data.item: These valuation techniques involve significant estimates and assumptions of unobservable inputs. Where the comparable trading multiples technique is used, the multiples are market related based on management’s judgement of comparable entities with similar businesses and then adjusted for discounts (marketability discounts) to determine an appropriate trading multiple. Where the cost method is used the fair value of underlying assets are used to derive the fair value of the unquoted investments. Changes in these inputs used in the valuation could also result in material adjustments to the carrying amounts of the unquoted investments and the record- ed gains/losses at year end. As a result of the above, the disclosures relating to the valuation of these complex financial instruments are also considered significant. We identified the valuation of unquoted investments as a key audit matter, due to the significant judgement involved in management’s use of unobservable valua- tion inputs and assumptions. • assess the appropriateness and consistency of the valua- tion methods used and the underlying key inputs such as the selected comparable revenue multiples, marketability discounts amongst others by comparing them to inde- pendent data sources. • For a sample of unquoted investments measured using the cost method, we performed independent valuations and compared the results to management’s fair value esti- mates, assessing the reasonableness of key assumptions and judgements applied. We assessed the appropriateness and adequacy of the disclo- sures related to the valuation of unquoted investments in the consolidated and separate financial statements, in accordance with IFRS 13, Fair Value Measurement.

data.item: As at the reporting date, the Group held investment properties amounting to Kshs 53.3 billion comprising of land and buildings measured at fair value. The Group uses external real estate valuers to de- termine the fair values of investment properties at year-end. The Group used the discounted cash flow method to value investment properties of buildings amounting to Kshs 4.2 billion and the market approach to value investment properties of land amounting to Kshs 49.1 billion. Our procedures included the following: • Evaluating the professional qualifications, competence, capabilities and objectivity of the external real estate valuers, employed by management, who valued the Group’s investment properties through inspection of their profes- sional membership and curriculum vita. • assessed management’s processes over the valuation of investment properties, including oversight from those charged with governance. • assessed the design and implementation of key controls related to the valuation process.

data.item: The fair value of the Group’s investment property (buildings) is classified as Level 3 in the fair value hierarchy, due to the use of unobservable inputs that involve inherent estimation uncertainty. The valuation under the discounted cash flow approach, involves significant estimates and assumptions of unobservable inputs in the valuation model such as projected future cash flows, future rent escalations, exit capitalisation rates and the discount rates. We identified the valuation of investment property using the discounted cash flow method, as a key audit matter due to the significant judgement and estimation involved in management’s use of unobservable inputs and assumptions. We engaged our own valuation specialists to assist with: • Evaluating the reasonableness of the inputs used in the discounted cash flow model. This included: » Assessing the accuracy of the projected future cash flows used in the valuation model to supporting lease contracts and historical expenditure patterns based on prior year actual costs and the projected inflationary adjustments to costs. » Challenging the appropriateness of the discount rates and exit capitalisation rates used in the valuation by comparing the discount rate to market rates and exit capitalisation rates to available industry data, taking into consideration comparability to housing indices and market factors. We assessed the appropriateness and adequacy of the disclosures related to the valuation of investment properties in the consolidated financial statements, in accordance with IFRS 13, Fair Value Measurement.
